subject: Vocabulary
topic: Prefixes — common Latin / Greek — mixed tiers
description: Anti-, dis-, pre-, post-, sub-, super-, trans-, mis-, re-, in- — meaning + word-formation

questions.stem: The prefix 'anti-' as in 'antibiotic', 'antidote', 'antigen' generally means:
questions.explanation: ANTI- (Greek) = against, opposed to. Antibiotic — substance that opposes life (specifically bacteria). Antidote — given against poison (Greek 'didonai' = to give). Antigen — substance that triggers antibody (originally 'antibody-generator'). Other examples: anti-clockwise, antiseptic, antithesis, antifreeze. Compare ANTE- (Latin, 'before') — antecedent, ante-meridiem (a.m.). Easy mnemonic: ANTI = against, ANTE = before, in time.

questions.stem: The prefix 'circum-' (as in circumnavigate, circumference, circumstance) means:
questions.explanation: CIRCUM- (Latin) = around. Circumnavigate — sail around (the world). Circumference — distance around a circle. Circumstance — situation 'standing around' (literally). Circumlocution — talking around (avoiding direct expression). Circumvent — go around (a problem). Related: 'circle', 'circus'. Trick: visualise a 'circle' to anchor any 'circum-' word.

questions.topic: Prefixes — common Latin / Greek — mixed tiers

questions.stem: What does the prefix 'mal-' mean in 'malnutrition', 'malice', 'malevolent'?
questions.explanation: MAL- (Latin 'malus' — bad). Malnutrition — bad/poor nutrition. Malice — wishing harm. Malevolent — wishing evil (compare benevolent — wishing good). Malign — speak ill of. Malignant tumour — cancerous, harmful. Maladjusted — poorly adjusted. Opposites usually take BENE- (Latin 'good'): benediction, benefactor, benevolent, beneficial. Pair them — 'malefactor' vs 'benefactor', 'malediction' vs 'benediction'.
questions.subject: Vocabulary
questions.topic: Prefixes — common Latin / Greek — mixed tiers

questions.explanation: PRE- (Latin 'prae'-) = before. Preview — see before. Predict — say before (it happens). Preheat — heat before (use). Pre-historic — before recorded history. Compare with POST- (after) — postwar, postpone, postscript. PRO- can mean 'forward' (proceed, project, propel) or 'in favour of' (pro-government, pro-active). RE- = again or back (review, return, revive).

questions.topic: Prefixes — common Latin / Greek — mixed tiers

questions.stem: Choose the word whose prefix means 'across' or 'beyond':
questions.explanation: TRANS- (Latin) = across, beyond, through. Transatlantic — across the Atlantic. Translate — carry meaning across languages. Transmit — send across. Transcend — climb beyond. Trans-Siberian, transgender, transparent. Other prefixes here: SUB- (under) — subterranean; PRE- (before) — prehistoric; INTER- (between) — international, intervene, intercept. SUPER- / SUPRA- (above) — supersonic, superintendent.

questions.topic: Prefixes — common Latin / Greek — mixed tiers

questions.stem: The Greek prefix 'auto-' as in 'autobiography', 'automatic', 'autonomy' means:
questions.explanation: AUTO- (Greek 'autos' — self). Autobiography — life-story written by oneself. Automatic — self-acting. Autonomy — self-rule. Autocrat — self-ruler (one who rules alone). Autograph — self-signature. Compare HOMO- (same) — homosexual, homogeneous, homonym; HETERO- (other / different) — heterogeneous, heterosexual; ALLO- (other) — allopathic, allotrope; PSEUDO- (false) — pseudonym, pseudocode.

questions.stem: Match prefix with meaning — which pairing is INCORRECT?
questions.explanation: DECA- means TEN, not hundred. Decade (10 years), decagon (10 sides), decimal, decathlon (10 events). HECTO- = hundred (hectolitre, hectare = 100 ares). Number-prefix series: uni- (1), bi- / di- (2), tri- (3), tetra- / quadr- (4), penta- / quint- (5), hexa- / sex- (6), hepta- / sept- (7), octa- / oct- (8), nona- / novem- (9), deca- / dec- (10), centi- / cent- (100), milli- / mille- (1000). Mostly Latin (numbers + measure) and Greek (figures).

questions.stem: In the words 'submarine', 'subtitle', and 'substandard', the Latin prefix 'sub-' conveys which core meaning?

options.option_text: across or through the middle of
beneath, below, or at a lower level
against or in opposition to something

questions.explanation: B is correct because 'sub-' is the Latin prefix meaning below or under: submarine = under the sea; subtitle = text below the main title; substandard = below the required standard. Option A ('across') describes 'trans-'; Option C ('between') belongs to 'inter-'; Option D ('against') is the meaning of 'anti-', which was the subject of a prior question.

questions.stem: The Latin prefix 'bene-' appears in 'benefit', 'benevolent', and 'benefactor'. What is its meaning?

options.option_text: bad, ill, or harmful in nature
before or prior to an occurrence
away from or without a quality

questions.explanation: D is correct: 'bene-' comes from Latin 'bonus' (good). 'Benefit' = something good received; 'benevolent' = wishing good to others; 'benefactor' = one who does good deeds. Option A describes 'mal-', the exact antonym prefix (malevolent, malice); this is the most tempting wrong choice because mal- and bene- form a classic pair.

questions.stem: The prefix 'mis-' in 'misnomer', 'misapprehend', and 'miscreant' consistently signals which meaning?

options.option_text: again or once more, as in repetition
less than or below the normal level
before or in anticipation of something

questions.explanation: B is correct: 'mis-' (Old English/Germanic) denotes wrongness or error. 'Misnomer' = wrong name; 'misapprehend' = understand incorrectly; 'miscreant' = one who behaves wrongly. Option A ('again/repeat') is the meaning of 're-' — a common confusion since 'mislead' could feel like 'leading again'. Option C ('below normal') belongs to 'under-' or 'sub-'.

questions.stem: A medical student confuses 'hyperglycaemia' (excess blood sugar) with 'hypoglycaemia' on an exam. The error turns on the prefix. What does the Greek prefix 'hypo-' mean?

options.option_text: many or multiple types of something
under, below, or less than normal
over, above, or more than the usual

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'hypo-' (Greek) means under or below normal — hypoglycaemia = blood sugar below normal; hypothermia = body temperature below normal. Option D ('over/above') actually describes 'hyper-', its direct opposite and the most tempting distractor. Option B ('around') describes 'peri-' (perimeter, pericardium), a prefix also common in medical terminology.

questions.stem: In 'extraordinary', 'extraterrestrial', and 'extravagant', the Latin prefix 'extra-' carries which meaning?

options.option_text: within or inside a bounded area
between two or more distinct groups
over and above, or outside the usual
before or earlier than the stated time

questions.explanation: C is correct: 'extra-' is Latin for 'outside of or beyond'. 'Extraordinary' = beyond the ordinary; 'extraterrestrial' = outside Earth; 'extravagant' = going beyond what is reasonable. Option A ('within') describes 'intra-' (intravenous, intramural) — the most frequent confusion since intra- and extra- are near-antonyms and look similar. Option D ('before') describes 'ante-' (antebellum, antenatal).

questions.stem: The Latin prefix 'ambi-' (ambiguous, ambidextrous, ambivalent) carries the sense of 'both' or 'on two sides'. Its closest Greek-origin equivalent, used in words like 'amphitheatre' and 'amphibian', is:

options.option_text: poly-, conveying many or several instances
amphi-, conveying both or on both sides
hetero-, conveying different or other kinds
mono-, conveying single or alone in class

questions.explanation: B is correct: Latin 'ambi-' and Greek 'amphi-' are cognates (both from PIE root meaning 'on both sides/around'). Amphitheatre = theatre with seating on both sides; amphibian = creature living in both water and land — exactly paralleling ambi-dextrous (both hands) and ambi-valent (both directions of feeling). Option A ('poly-') means many, not two; Option D ('mono-') means one — the opposite pole.

questions.stem: The Greek prefix 'syn-/sym-' means 'together or with' (synthesis, syndrome, symmetry). Which of the following uses a DIFFERENT prefix that also means 'together' but is of Latin — not Greek — origin?
questions.explanation: B is correct: 'com-/con-' is the Latin prefix meaning 'together/with' — composite = put together, compound = placed together, collaborate = work together. The other three options (symposium, synchrony, syndrome) all use Greek 'syn-/sym-', the same family named in the stem, so none of them qualifies as a Latin equivalent. The question tests the ability to distinguish Greek and Latin cognate prefixes that share a meaning — a pattern frequently exploited in SSC and banking vocabulary sections.
